column7: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
column10: A 68-year-old man has unfavorable intermediate-risk localized prostate cancer and an estimated life expectancy of 15 years. Which treatment choice should be offered according to the AUA/ASTRO guideline?
column12: Radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy plus androgen deprivation therapy
column13: Active surveillance as the preferred option
column14: Focal ablation outside a clinical trial
column17: Option B is correct. For patients with unfavorable intermediate- or high-risk localized prostate cancer and life expectancy greater than 10 years, clinicians should offer a choice between radical prostatectomy or radiation therapy plus androgen deprivation therapy. Option A is incorrect because androgen deprivation alone is not the preferred definitive treatment in a patient with long life expectancy. Option C is incorrect because active surveillance is not the recommended approach for this higher-risk group. Option D is incorrect because focal ablation lacks the evidence base to replace standard definitive therapy here. Option E is incorrect because delaying treatment until metastases develop forfeits the chance for curative local therapy. Teaching point: Higher-risk localized prostate cancer with substantial life expectancy warrants definitive local treatment rather than surveillance or palliative therapy. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

column7: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
column10: A man has a detectable PSA after radical prostatectomy and is being considered for salvage radiation therapy. At what PSA level should salvage radiation be provided according to the AUA/ASTRO/SUO guideline?
column13: When the PSA is 0.5 ng/mL or lower
column14: When PSA doubling time is less than 3 months regardless of PSA level
column15: After a trial of androgen deprivation therapy
column17: Option C is correct. The salvage therapy guideline recommends providing salvage radiation when the PSA is 0.5 ng/mL or lower in patients with a detectable PSA after radical prostatectomy who are candidates for salvage treatment. Option A is incorrect because waiting for a PSA above 2.0 ng/mL delays treatment beyond the recommended threshold. Option B is incorrect because a positive bone scan is not required before appropriately timed salvage radiation. Option D is incorrect because PSA doubling time informs risk but does not replace the PSA threshold recommendation. Option E is incorrect because salvage radiation should not be deferred until androgen deprivation therapy fails. Teaching point: Salvage radiation is most effective when delivered early in biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

column7: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
column10: An intermediate-risk non-muscle invasive bladder cancer patient has a complete response after induction BCG. What maintenance approach should be considered according to the AUA/SUO guideline?
column11: Maintenance BCG for one year, as tolerated
column12: No further intravesical therapy under any circumstance
column13: Immediate radical cystectomy for routine responders
column14: Monthly office fulguration instead of surveillance
column15: Systemic chemotherapy instead of maintenance intravesical therapy
column17: Option A is correct. In an intermediate-risk patient who completely responds to induction BCG, clinicians should consider maintenance BCG for one year as tolerated. Option B is incorrect because the guideline specifically supports considering maintenance therapy after response. Option C is incorrect because radical cystectomy is not the routine next step for an intermediate-risk complete responder. Option D is incorrect because office fulguration does not replace guideline-based maintenance planning and surveillance. Option E is incorrect because systemic chemotherapy has no routine role in this setting. Teaching point: Intermediate-risk NMIBC responders to induction BCG often remain on one year of maintenance BCG rather than stopping therapy immediately. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

column7: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
column10: A recurrent calcium stone former keeps forming stones despite appropriate diet counseling and no remaining metabolic abnormality on 24-hour urine testing. Which preventive therapy does the AUA guideline support?
column13: Routine urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate
column17: Option D is correct. For recurrent calcium stone formers in whom other metabolic abnormalities are absent or have already been addressed, the guideline supports thiazide diuretics and/or potassium citrate to reduce further stone formation. Option A is incorrect because antibiotic prophylaxis does not prevent recurrent calcium stones. Option B is incorrect because loop diuretics can increase urinary calcium excretion rather than prevent calcium stones. Option C is incorrect because sodium bicarbonate alone is not the specific recommendation for persistent recurrent calcium stones without a defined residual abnormality. Option E is incorrect because tamsulosin may help passage of some stones but does not serve as long-term recurrence prevention. Teaching point: Persistent calcium stone recurrence can justify pharmacologic prevention even when a clear residual urinary abnormality is not found. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

column7: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
column10: A calcium stone former has relatively high urinary calcium on 24-hour urine testing. Which diet advice best matches the AUA guideline?
column12: Increase sodium intake to improve urine output
column13: Use calcium supplements without a full dietary review
column15: Limit sodium intake and maintain 1,000 to 1,200 mg/day of dietary calcium
column17: Option E is correct. Patients with calcium stones and relatively high urinary calcium should be counseled to limit sodium intake while maintaining normal dietary calcium intake of about 1,000 to 1,200 mg daily. Option A is incorrect because severe calcium restriction can worsen stone risk and is not the guideline recommendation. Option B is incorrect because higher sodium intake increases urinary calcium excretion. Option C is incorrect because supplementation without dietary assessment is not the core recommendation and can worsen supersaturation in some patients. Option D is incorrect because fruit and vegetable restriction does not address hypercalciuria and may worsen other stone-risk factors. Teaching point: Hypercalciuric stone prevention focuses on sodium restriction plus normal dietary calcium, not calcium elimination. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

column7: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
column10: A woman presents with urgency, frequency, and urgency urinary incontinence, and her history, exam, and urinalysis support idiopathic overactive bladder. Which test should not be performed routinely during the initial evaluation?
column12: Urodynamics, cystoscopy, or urinary tract imaging
column17: Option B is correct. The OAB guideline states that clinicians should not routinely perform urodynamics, cystoscopy, or urinary tract imaging in the initial evaluation of patients with overactive bladder. Option A is incorrect because urinalysis is part of the recommended initial evaluation. Option C is incorrect because physical examination remains a core initial step. Option D is incorrect because detailed bladder symptom assessment is required to establish the clinical syndrome. Option E is incorrect because contributing comorbid conditions should be assessed during evaluation. Teaching point: OAB is primarily a clinical diagnosis, so advanced testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or atypical findings. Source: American Urological Association. column7: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
column10: A patient with bothersome overactive bladder symptoms has already tried bladder training. Which medication classes should be offered next to improve urgency, frequency, and urgency urinary incontinence?
column11: Chronic suppressive antibiotics or alpha blockers alone
column15: No medication because oral therapy is ineffective for OAB
column17: Option C is correct. The AUA/SUFU guideline recommends offering antimuscarinic medications or beta-3 agonists to improve urgency, frequency, and urgency urinary incontinence in patients with overactive bladder. Option A is incorrect because those drugs do not represent standard oral OAB pharmacotherapy. Option B is incorrect because chemotherapy and corticosteroids do not treat idiopathic OAB. Option D is incorrect because invasive reconstruction is not the next step after behavioral therapy. Option E is incorrect because oral OAB medications do provide symptom benefit for many patients. Teaching point: After behavioral therapy, OAB pharmacotherapy centers on antimuscarinic and beta-3 agonist options chosen through shared decision-making. Source: American Urological Association. column10: A low-risk patient with microhematuria undergoes repeat urinalysis at 6 months and still has persistent microhematuria. What is the next step under the AUA/SUFU guideline?
column11: Reclassify the patient as intermediate- or high-risk and perform risk-based evaluation
column12: Continue periodic urinalysis without risk reclassification
column13: Discharge the patient because one repeat urinalysis is sufficient
column14: Start empiric antibiotics before any further evaluation
column17: Option A is correct. Low-risk patients with persistent microhematuria on repeat urinalysis should be reclassified as intermediate- or high-risk and then undergo the corresponding risk-based evaluation. Option B is incorrect because persistent hematuria should trigger escalation rather than indefinite observation. Option C is incorrect because persistence on repeat testing does not end the evaluation. Option D is incorrect because empiric antibiotics are not the guideline response to persistent risk-stratified microhematuria without evidence of infection. Option E is incorrect because nephrectomy evaluation is not the default next step in this scenario. Teaching point: Persistent microhematuria after an initially low-risk presentation changes the patient’s risk category and the downstream workup. Source: American Urological Association. column7: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
column10: A man with chronic pelvic pain is found to have pelvic floor myalgia on examination. Which treatment may be offered according to the AUA guideline?
column14: Individualized manual physical therapy such as myofascial release
column17: Option D is correct. In men with pelvic floor myalgia or abdominopelvic muscle myalgia, clinicians may offer individualized manual physical therapy techniques such as internal and external myofascial release. Option A is incorrect because long-term systemic glucocorticoids should not be used to treat chronic pelvic pain. Option B is incorrect because orchiectomy does not treat pelvic floor myalgia. Option C is incorrect because chronic catheterization does not address the myofascial pain mechanism. Option E is incorrect because radical prostatectomy has no routine role in treating pelvic floor myalgia. Teaching point: Pelvic floor myalgia is a treatable pain phenotype that often responds better to targeted pelvic physical therapy than to surgery or empiric systemic medication. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.

column7: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
column10: A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman has recurrent uncomplicated UTIs and no contraindication to estrogen. Which preventive therapy should be recommended according to the AUA/CUA/SUFU guideline?
column13: Chronic fluoroquinolone prophylaxis as routine first-line prevention
column14: Routine upper-tract imaging after each infection
column17: Option E is correct. In peri- and postmenopausal women with recurrent uncomplicated UTIs, clinicians should recommend vaginal estrogen therapy when there is no contraindication in order to reduce future infections. Option A is incorrect because corticosteroids do not prevent recurrent uncomplicated UTI. Option B is incorrect because routine cystoscopy is not recommended for the index recurrent UTI patient. Option C is incorrect because chronic fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is not the universal first-line preventive recommendation for all such patients. Option D is incorrect because routine upper-tract imaging is not part of standard preventive management. Teaching point: Vaginal estrogen is a guideline-supported nonantibiotic prevention strategy for hypoestrogenic women with recurrent UTI. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
